articles.title: Reciprocal Miscalibration in Personalized AI Correction. User model fidelity persuasive fit and feedback over time
articles.abstract: Persistent AI agents can condition advice and correction on disclosures, histories, and inferred preferences. Apparent personalization fit is insufficient evidence of calibration. A system may misrepresent its user while the user poorly distinguishes accurate from inaccurate advice; their coexistence is termed dual miscalibration. Reciprocal miscalibration is a narrower hypothesis: representation-conditioned outputs affect behaviour, that behaviour updates the operative representation, and the updated state sustains or worsens both representation error and miscalibrated human reliance. The framework separates user-model fidelity, contextual representation fit, perceived fit, persuasive efficacy, and advice accuracy. An accurate record of a false user belief remains distinct from endorsing that belief as true. Performative prediction, preference pollution, persuasion profiling, distributed cognition, narrative railroading, and human-AI feedback research supply direct antecedents. The contribution is an operational refinement of these problems for conversational correction, with falsifiable propositions and interventions on representation updating and correction. Feedback to the human about independently checked outcomes is distinguished from behaviour fed back into the system. A factorial study tests immediate effects; a longitudinal intervention tests reciprocal reinforcement. Appropriate reliance additionally depends on payoffs, checking costs, relative competence, and learning opportunities. Neither reciprocity nor the benefit of the proposed controls has been established by this conceptual synthesis.

articles.title: ScholarForge AI: An Open, Multi-Agent RAG Platform for Automated Research Paper Analysis
articles.abstract: The growing volume of scientific literature has made research-paper analysis increasingly time-consuming for students, researchers, and academicians. Tasks such as literature review generation, methodology understanding, research gap identification, citation formatting, and trend discovery often require substantial manual effort. To address these challenges, this paper presents ScholarForge AI, an open, multi-agent Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform designed to automate research-paper analysis and transform scholarly documents into actionable research intelligence. The proposed system integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), LangGraph-based multi-agent orchestration, ChromaDB vector storage, a Neo4j knowledge graph, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to support intelligent document processing. Research papers in PDF format are processed using PyMuPDF and EasyOCR, then chunked and embedded with the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 sentence transformer model for semantic retrieval. The platform includes specialized agents for literature review generation, methodology analysis, research gap detection, trend analysis, research idea generation, citation formatting, interactive question answering and difficulty prediction. In addition, a research difficulty predictor classifies papers as Easy, Medium, or Hard, while the knowledge graph visualizes relationships among papers, authors, keywords, methods, and topics. Experimental results show that ScholarForge AI improves the efficiency of literature survey preparation, supports accurate gap identification, and provides context-aware research recommendations. Built entirely on open-source technologies, the platform offers a scalable and accessible solution for academic research support.

articles.title: CreatorMemBench v1.0: A Lifecycle Benchmark for Mutable Creator-Agent Memory
articles.abstract: CreatorMemBench v1.0 contains 20 synthetic creator timelines and 160 checkpoints for evaluating mutable long-term memory in creator agents. The benchmark covers stable identity, scoped preferences, multi-session composition, transient noise, updates, forgetting, retention, and resurrection. The archive includes separated inputs and gold criteria, a strict semantic scoring protocol, an offline aggregation script, a prediction schema, a license, and SHA-256 checksums. It contains no production conversations, account identifiers, credentials, proprietary service code, endpoint identifiers, or raw internal traces.

articles.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
articles.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.

articles.title: Data and code for: Who wins depends on who judges: re-grading published LoCoMo and LongMemEval answers of agent memory systems
articles.abstract: Verdicts, labels, tables and code for a study of how published long-term memory leaderboards for LLM agents depend on the LLM judge. The 47,253 unique answers that vendors and third parties published for 50 answer sets (36 LoCoMo, 14 LongMemEval-S; 10 memory products and 9 baselines) were re-graded by a grid of 20 judge configurations (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini and gpt-5-mini on both benchmarks, gpt-4o on LongMemEval-S only, each with five prompts): 737,115 verdicts. A reference judge (gpt-5.4, reasoning effort low) graded 5,000 of the answers under the same five prompts: 25,000 verdicts. 250 disputed answers carry three-way labels (CORRECT, PARTIAL, WRONG) from an LLM annotator in two independent blind passes; these are model labels, not human labels. Question, gold and answer texts and raw judge replies are not included, because they belong to the benchmark authors and the vendors or can quote them. Every key resolves to the public source files listed with URL, commit and SHA-256 in code/manifest.json, and the included code rebuilds the aligned answers. See README.md.

articles.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
articles.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent long-term memory, which creates a critical vulnerability that we study here: memory poisoning. An adversary can store untrusted content in one session that later steers a consequential action, such as a payment, a setting change, or data exfiltration, in a future session. Existing defenses base a memory item's authority to act on either its content (detection or trust-scoring) or its derivation history (lineage). We show that both signals are malleable. An attacker can launder an untrusted origin through three channels specific to LLM agents: the agent's own summarization, a trusted-tool echo, and manufactured corroboration. Each makes the content look benign and breaks or flips its derivation edge to ``trusted.'' We formalize malleability for the memory write-retrieve-act pipeline and prove a machine-checked separation theorem. No content- or lineage-based defense is sound under laundering (T1), write-time origin binding is necessary (T2), and non-malleable origin-bound authority with Sybil-resistant corroboration-gated elevation is sufficient (T3). Our construction, TMA-NM (Tamper-evident Memory Authority, Non-Malleable), instantiates non-malleable information-flow control (IFC) for LLM-agent memory. A cross-defense, cross-attack, and cross-model benchmark over eight frontier models shows that existing defenses fail exactly where the theory predicts (up to 68% laundering attack-success), while TMA-NM reaches 0% attack success on both direct and laundering attacks across all models and channels, at full legitimate utility. We release the benchmark, harness, and machine-checked TLA+ models to support reproducibility.

articles.title: MemMark: State-Evolution Attribution Watermarking for Agent Long-Term Memory Systems
articles.abstract: Memory-backed agents need provenance that can survive leaked or migrated snapshots, where logs, visible outputs, and trusted metadata may be absent. We propose MemMark, a state-evolution attribution watermark that embeds an owner-controlled signal into latent memory-write decisions. At each internal LLM call, MemMark samples among admissible candidates using keyed, distribution-preserving selection, and records cryptographic commitments with signed session anchors and reveal evidence. This makes attribution depend on reproducible backend behavior rather than mutable provenance fields. Across A-Mem and Graphiti on LoCoMo, with three LLM backbones, MemMark preserves memory utility: Overall F1 retains 99.6% of the unwatermarked baseline, while BLEU-1 changes by +0.2%. It also provides usable carrier capacity, with 1.16, 1.14, and 1.26 bits of mean entropy for update-target, link-target, and semantic-realization decisions. In the snapshot-only R3 setting, MemMark recovers the full 40-bit payload from final snapshots, while wrong-key verification remains near chance. Under nine memory-lifecycle attacks, verification distinguishes tampering, evidence deletion, and partial payload recovery. These results show that robust snapshot-only attribution is feasible for long-term agent memory without surviving traces, trusted metadata, or utility-degrading.

articles.title: Fairness Vs. Personalization: Towards Equity in Epistemic Utility
articles.abstract: Personalized recommender systems are rapidly expanding in applications across the web, encompassing social media, online shopping, search engine results, and more. Personalization provides significant value in navigating the vast array of items available, as it can help to disambiguate search terms and generally provide more accurate recommendations. However, alongside this growth, there has been increased recognition of the potential for algorithmic systems to exhibit and perpetuate biases. In particular, personalized recommender systems may risk unfairness in recommendations, leading to biases in access to information and epistemic utility. In this work, we differentiate between idealized and realized notions of personalization in the extreme to motivate our fairness definition: an equity-based approach to epistemic utility. Our approach bypasses many issues with comparative notions of fairness and instead aims to guarantee all users baseline access to information. We discuss key trade-offs and challenges for operationalizing our definition and provide policy recommendations towards achieving fairness in personalized systems.

articles.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
articles.abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

articles.title: AI AS A CHOICE ARCHITECT: ETHICAL IMPLICATIONS OF ALGORITHMIC NUDGING IN ONLINE RETAIL
articles.abstract: Nudge Theory, introduced by Thaler and Sunstein in their seminal book, inspired the creation of human choice architects who applied behavioural insights into influence decisions across various domains. In the online retail industry, however, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, predictive analytics, and real time data personalization has transformed traditional nudging into algorithmic choice architecture powered by data-driven insights. This paper conceptually examines how AI driven Algorithmic nudges operate through cross- platform behavioural tracking, recommender systems, push notifications, and default designs to influence consumer decisions. The epistemological orientation of this paper is grounded in qualitative and interpretative approach based on critical realism to explore how consumers conform to stacked and multichannel nudges(multiple, sequential interventions across apps, websites and social platforms) that leverage cognitive biases and bounded rationality. Findings suggest that AI enabled nudges outperform human- designed ones in precision, scalability, and contextual adaptability, allowing retailers to subtly guide consumer behaviour under the guise of personalisation. However, the opacity of these algorithmic mechanisms raises serious ethical questions regarding informed consent, privacy, and autonomy, especially for vulnerable consumer groups. The study underscores the need for transparent AI governance, ethical design principles, and regulatory frameworks to prevent behavioural manipulation in digital marketplaces. It further argues that the evolution from libertarian paternalism to algorithmic paternalism represents a critical shift that challenges the foundational ethics of Nudge Theory and calls for cross-disciplinary collaboration between marketing, technology, human- computer interaction and law to ensure responsible AI-driven persuasion in online retail.

articles.title: Perceived personalization of social media ads and online compulsive purchase
articles.abstract: The increasing integration of social networking, online shopping, and personalized advertising has created a digital environment in which consumers are continuously exposed to consumption-related cues. This study examines the effects of heavy social networking, financial social comparison, materialism, and perceived personalization of social media ads on online compulsive purchase. It further investigates whether perceived personalization of social media ads strengthen the effects of heavy social networking, financial social comparison, and materialism on online compulsive purchase. Data were collected from 361 consumers in Türkiye and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The results show that financial social comparison, heavy social networking, materialism, and Perceived Personalization of Social Media Ads all have significant positive effects on online compulsive purchase. Financial social comparison has the strongest effect, followed closely by heavy social networking and materialism, while the direct effect of Perceived Personalization of Social Media Ads is comparatively smaller. Contrary to expectations, Perceived Personalization of Social Media Ads do not significantly moderate any of the three proposed relationships. The model explains 50.2% of the variance in online compulsive purchase, and PLSpredict and CVPAT results further support its out-of-sample predictive ability. The findings indicate that personalized advertising contributes directly to online compulsive purchase rather than intensifying the effects of consumers’ social networking, financial comparison, or materialistic tendencies. The study provides a more differentiated understanding of how consumer-related factors and personalized advertising operate together in online compulsive purchasing.

articles.title: Testing Personalization in LLM-Based Mental Health Support: A Proposed Experimental Design for College Students
articles.abstract: Rising student mental health demand has outpaced campus counseling capacity. This paper proposes a 2x2 between-subjects experimental design to test whether a personalized LLM-based chatbot, grounded in just-in-time adaptive intervention principles and cognitive load theory, provides better short-term anxiety reduction than a standard chatbot across stress and neutral contexts. The personalized chatbot uses wearable stress data, sleep quality, self-reported overwhelm, and support preferences to select between low-load and elaborative support paths. The design contributes a practical framework for evaluating personalization in AI-driven mental health tools and informs scalable, responsible institutional deployment.

articles.title: Designing the evidence base and user-needs framework for a digital health intervention supporting sleep and screen-time behaviors in young adults
articles.abstract: Background Background. Insufficient and disturbed sleep is common among young adults and evening and in-bed smartphone use is widespread and associated with poorer sleep outcomes. Young adults combine high need with high reachability through digital channels. However, they receive little age-specific guidance, because they fall between recommendations written for children and adolescents and those written for adults in general. Digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) appears effective in this population, and guided interventions tend to outperform unguided ones. Artificial intelligence (AI) may combine some of the benefits of guidance with greater scalability, for example through conversational agents, data-driven personalisation or just-in-time adaptive interventions. At the same time, it raises questions of trust, transparency and data governance. No one has yet systematically mapped the evidence on digital interventions that target sleep and evening screen use in this age group, including their use of human guidance and AI, user engagement, and young adults’ own perspectives. Objective. This scoping review aims to map the available evidence on digital interventions developed or evaluated to improve sleep and reduce evening screen use among young adults aged 18–25 years. These include apps, websites, chatbots and conversational agents, wearables, and text or messaging services. The review addresses five questions: 1. What digital interventions (apps, websites, chatbots, conversational agents, wearables, messaging) have been developed or evaluated to improve sleep and reduce evening screen use among young adults, and what are their components (e.g., CBT-I, sleep hygiene, screen-reduction strategies), delivery models, level of human guidance and use of AI (e.g., conversational support, personalization, just-in-time adaptation)? 2. Which sleep, screen-use and secondary outcomes (mental health, academic performance, quality of life) are reported, how are they measured (subjective vs. Objective, validated instruments), what effects are reported (including clinically meaningful change or remission), and are these effects maintained at follow-up? 3. What is reported on adherence, engagement, attrition, and which intervention features are (e.g., human guidance, reminders, personalization, AI) are reported alongside higher or lower engagement? 4. What needs, preferences, barriers, facilitators and acceptability judgements do young adults report regarding digital sleep and screen-use support, including preferences on timing, interaction style, human support, trust, transparency and data sharing, and, where reported, how do these vary across groups (e.g., gender, students vs. workers, socioeconomic status)? Secondary sub-question (grey literature search of guidelines) 5.What clinical, sleep-health and screen-use recommendations are available from international and national guideline authorities (e.g. WHO, NSF, AASM, ESRS, national authorities) to inform a digital intervention for young adults, what do they specify for digital interventions, and what is the strength and applicability of these recommendations to this age group? RQ5 is treated as a secondary question because it does not map the intervention evidence itself. Instead, it provides the normative benchmark against which the interventions (RQ1-RQ4) and the survey findings (RQ6-RQ7) are interpreted. Methods. The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to PRISMA-ScR, with the search reported according to PRISMA-S. Eligibility is defined with the Population–Concept–Context framework: Population: young adults aged 18-25 years. A study qualifies if all participants are in this range, if the mean or median age falls within it, or if results are reported separately for this group. Eligible samples include students, workers, and people with insomnia symptoms, short or irregular sleep, or problematic smartphone use. Concept: digital interventions (unguided, guided or blended) aiming to improve sleep and/or reduce evening screen use that report at least one sleep, screen-use, engagement or user-perspective outcome. Context: any country and setting. Eligible source types are randomised and non-randomised trials; pre–post, feasibility, pilot and usability studies; development and co-design studies; and qualitative, mixed-methods and survey studies of needs or preferences. MEDLINE (PubMed), APA PsycInfo and Scopus will be searched for English-language sources published from January 2000 onwards. The reference lists of included sources and relevant reviews will then be screened. Screening will take place in Rayyan in two stages: titles and abstracts, then full texts. It starts with a calibration phase in which two reviewers independently screen a random 25% of records (target agreement ≥75%). A second reviewer will verify all full-text exclusions and borderline records, and a third reviewer will resolve any remaining disagreements. In line with scoping review methodology, no formal critical appraisal will be conducted. Results will be synthesised descriptively through tables, charts and narrative summary. Guidelines are identified through a separate search with its own eligibility criteria, so they are not included in the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. They are reported separately as a supplementary evidence stream. Expected outcomes. The review will produce a structured overview of existing digital interventions for sleep and evening screen use in young adults. It will cover their components, delivery, human guidance and AI use, how outcomes and engagement have been measured, what users report needing and preferring, and which guideline recommendations apply to this age group. The review is also expected to identify gaps in the evidence, such as limited use of objective measures, short follow-up periods, or scarce evaluation of AI-supported and screen-use components. Findings will be interpreted in relation to the WHAT criteria (Work, Help, Accessible, Trusted) of the European Insomnia Guideline. The review is Study 1 of an MSc thesis at Wageningen University & Research. Its findings will be integrated with a cross-sectional survey of young adults (Study 2, which serves as the stakeholder consultation stage) to derive requirements for the future design of a trustworthy, AI-assisted digital intervention for sleep and evening screen use.

articles.title: Bridging design disciplines: a literature review of biologically-inspired design, human-centered design, and human-robot interaction
articles.abstract: Abstract As robotic technologies become more integrated into society, there is a growing demand for systems that are not only technically robust, but also socially accepted, safe, and designed for long-term use. Biologically-Inspired Design (BID), Human-Centered Design (HCD), and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) each offer valuable theories, methodologies, and tools to support the design and evaluation of such systems. Despite their complementary goals, these fields have largely developed in isolation. The lack of integration across BID, HCD, and HRI presents significant barriers for researchers and designers seeking to create biologically-informed, human-centered robots that facilitate meaningful interactions. In this work, an integrative literature review was conducted to examine the fields of BID, HCD, and HRI. An analytic categorization approach was used to categorize 63 papers into one or more of the three fields: 20 in BID, 27 in HCD, and 21 in HRI, with some papers categorized into multiple categories. Within each field, an inductive, interpretive coding and thematic analysis were used to identify key terminology, tools, methods, and conceptual frameworks, helping establish a shared vocabulary and summarize the state of the art. This was followed by a synthesis of limitations and field-specific gaps. Cross-field analysis revealed only four papers demonstrating overlap within the reviewed corpus: three showing implicit connections between HCD and HRI, and one showing implicit overlap between BID and HRI with indirect ties to HCD. This review lays the groundwork for more integrated design research by identifying opportunities for collaboration across BID, HCD, and HRI, highlighting the potential for more biologically-informed, user-centered, and socially responsive robotic systems.

articles.title: LLM-based multi-agent systems for code generation: A multi-vocal literature review
articles.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled multi-agent systems to perform autonomous code generation for complex tasks. Despite the recent growth in research and industrial applications in this area, there is little work on synthesizing evidence from both academic and industrial sources to capture the current state of research on LLM-based multi-agent systems for code generation. To this end, we conducted a Multi-Vocal Literature Review (MLR), combining insights from both academia and industry, including peer-reviewed studies and grey literature. The aim of this study is to systematically synthesize and analyze existing knowledge on LLM-based multi-agent systems for code generation. Specifically, the review examines the motivations for their use, employed benchmarks and models, key challenges, proposed solutions, and potential directions for future research. We selected and reviewed 114 studies, and the key findings are: (1) the identified reasons for adopting multi-agent systems for code generation were classified into nine categories; (2) the models and evaluation benchmarks utilized across the studies were systematically analyzed to provide a structured overview of commonly adopted LLM configurations and assessment practices; (3) the reported challenges and corresponding solutions were synthesized into seven main categories and 26 subcategories; and (4) future research directions were identified and organized into six main categories and 18 subcategories. The results of this MLR will assist researchers and practitioners in pursuing further studies and supporting the real-world adoption of multi-agent systems in industrial settings.

articles.title: Human-AI Collaboration and Organizational Adaptation: Insights from Knowledge Workers in Banten, Indonesia
articles.abstract: This qualitative descriptive study explores how Human-AI collaboration shapes organizational adaptation among knowledge workers in Banten, Indonesia. Using multi-case inquiry with 20 purposively selected participants comprising knowledge workers, middle managers, senior managers, and digital transformation leaders, this research employed semi-structured interviews, organizational document analysis, and observation protocols. Thematic analysis revealed four critical patterns: (1) AI integration reshapes collaborative workflows through augmentation rather than replacement; (2) knowledge work transformation emerges through new competency demands and skill reconfiguration; (3) organizational learning accelerates through human-AI knowledge co-creation; and (4) adaptive organizational practices evolve through dynamic capability reconfiguration. The study contributes theoretically by extending dynamic capability theory, organizational adaptation theory, and knowledge-based view through an emerging economy lens, demonstrating that Human-AI collaboration functions as a mechanism for organizational adaptation when complemented by deliberate knowledge management systems, adaptive leadership, and human-centric learning cultures. Practically, findings offer strategic guidance for organizational leaders, human resource managers, and policymakers navigating AI-driven transformation in knowledge-intensive sectors. This research uniquely addresses the gap between AI adoption studies and organizational adaptation processes, providing nuanced understanding of Human-AI collaboration in an emerging economy context where institutional support and digital literacy remain evolving. The novelty lies in positioning Human-AI collaboration as central to organizational adaptation rather than treating it as a peripheral technological implementation concern, with particular relevance to organizations in Southeast Asian emerging markets.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and anti-cancer drugs: advancing discovery, personalization, and precision oncology
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way we discover anticancer drugs. It tackles the problems of traditional methods, such as prolonged timelines for drug development, higher costs, and substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. This review explains how AI is applied throughout the cancer drug pipeline. This includes target identification, virtual screening of compounds, molecular docking, and predicting pharmacokinetics. We explore how machine learning models speed up hit-to-lead optimization, improve clinical trial design by stratifying patients, and allow for real-time toxicity monitoring. A key focus is on integrating AI with multi-omics data, including proteomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, to support precision oncology and personalized treatments. We address important validation challenges, like model interpretability, data quality, and regulatory issues that must be solved before AI can be widely used in clinics. By summarizing current evidence and targeting research gaps, this review offers a clear view of how AI is enhancing the discovery, personalization, and validation of anticancer treatments.

articles.title: Explanation User Interfaces: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is one of the major technological advancements of this century, bearing incredible potential for users through AI-powered applications and tools in numerous domains. Being often black-box (i.e., its decision-making process is unintelligible), developers typically resort to eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to interpret the behavior of AI models to produce systems that are transparent, fair, reliable, and trustworthy. However, presenting explanations to the user is not trivial and is often left as a secondary aspect of the system’s design process, leading to AI systems that are not useful to end-users. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review on Explanation User Interfaces (XUIs) to gain a deeper understanding of the solutions and design guidelines employed in the academic literature to effectively present explanations to users. To improve the contribution and real-world impact of this survey, we also present a platform to support Human-cEnteRed developMent of Explainable user interfaceS (HERMES) and guide practitioners and scholars in the design and evaluation of XUIs.

articles.title: Case Report: Neonatal ultra-severe hemolytic anemia complicated by pulmonary hypertension induced by compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene and literature review
articles.abstract: Objective To investigate the clinical characteristics, genotypic profiles, and diagnostic/therapeutic strategies for congenital hemolytic anemia induced by compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene. Methods We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of a neonate who presented primarily with ultra-severe anemia, elevated direct bilirubin, and pulmonary hypertension. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was utilized for variant identification, followed by a comprehensive review of literature. Results The patient, a female neonate, developed severe anemia within 10 h of birth, accompanied by rapidly progressing hyperbilirubinemia (predominantly direct hyperbilirubinemia). Bedside echocardiography revealed a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary hypertension. Trio-WES identified pathogenic compound heterozygous variants in the KLF1 gene: c.519_525dup (p.Gly176ArgfsTer179) and c.1012C > A (p.Pro338Thr). Following multiple red blood cell transfusions and mechanical ventilatory support, the infant's condition stabilized. During a 24-month follow-up, the patient exhibited transfusion-dependent anemia. Conclusion For neonates presenting with unexplained (Coombs/DAT-negative) severe hemolytic anemia, particularly when complicated by pulmonary hypertension and atypical cholestasis, early genetic testing should be performed to rule out KLF1 -related diseases.

articles.title: Identifying Harm in Personalized, Generative AI Systems Requires User-Centered Auditing at the Interaction Level
articles.abstract: Personalized, generative AI systems increasingly adapt their behavior to individual users over time, fundamentally changing model behavior. While existing auditing approaches have been effective at surfacing harms in non-personalized contexts, they often rely on static, simulated evaluations and definitions of harm that aggregate across broad, group categories. In this position paper, we argue that such approaches can fail to capture emergent harms in personalized generative AI systems, where harms surface through interpretations of ongoing interaction and evolve with user history. We identify three presuppositions underlying many harm auditing paradigms: that harms can be (1) specified outside real-world interaction, (2) defined non-pluralistically within groups, and (3) treated as static. One might argue that personalized systems could simply learn definitions of what constitutes harm to individual users through repeated interactions. However, we argue that attempts to surface user harms through deeper personalization risk imposing asymmetric burdens of labor and privacy on marginalized users. Consequently, we propose reframing understandings of harm as adaptive, user- and community-centered processes, and outline design directions that shift auditing from retrospective evaluation toward infrastructures that support ongoing articulation of harm in interaction. Our work highlights the need for auditing and design practices that better reflect the pluralistic and evolving nature of harm understanding in personalized generative AI systems.

articles.title: Autonomous AI research agents in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma immunology: from multimodal evidence to experimental validation
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational–experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.

articles.title: What to Keep, What to Forget: A Rate--Distortion View of Memory Compaction in LLMs and Agents
articles.abstract: Large language models, and the agents built on them, spend an ever-growing share of their compute and memory on remembering: caching attention keys and values, carrying long prompts, maintaining recurrent state, and storing what happened in previous turns and sessions. Because none of this memory is free, four largely separate research communities have each learned to compact it. They evict or quantize the KV cache, prune or distill prompts, bound architectural state, and consolidate agent memory. We argue that these are instances of one problem: a rate--distortion decision about what context-derived information to retain versus discard, at what fidelity, under a resource budget, so as to preserve downstream task utility. We make this lens precise with a single compaction objective and a layer-agnostic lower bound, use it to build a seven-axis taxonomy that classifies methods from across the stack uniformly, and use it to transfer mechanisms between layers that have never been connected, from serving-stack KV management to agent long-term memory. Two patterns hold across the survey. At every layer the signal that decides what to keep is attention magnitude or recency, and it fails in the same way everywhere, by discarding, before the query is known and with no way to undo it, information the query later needs. And while compression is measured carefully on single-turn long context, the repeated compaction that agents actually perform is almost never measured, and no benchmark holds one budget axis across all the layers at once. We turn both observations into a benchmark proposal, a small reference experiment, and a set of compaction-aware design principles, and we map the open problems.

articles.title: Persistent Semantic Agency: An Architecture for Agent Systems Beyond the Loop
articles.abstract: Persistent Semantic Agency argues that the architectural center of an intelligent agent system must move from the trajectory of a model to a persistent semantic system of delegated commitments, structured work, knowledge, memory, responsibility, authority, and evidence. Models reason inside that system; they do not constitute it. This technical manifesto and reference architecture develops a domain-independent model for long-horizon agent systems. It introduces Commitment as the unit of durable agency; a typed semantic Work Intermediate Representation (Work IR); explicit Unknowns, Decisions, Responsibility, Delegation, Authority, and Evidence; a strict separation of Memory, Knowledge, State, and Context; dynamic composition of models, humans, solvers, compilers, knowledge sources, and organizations as cognitive and execution Resources; and proposal/admission, independent observation, verification, acceptance, and derived Closure as the governing transition model. The publication comprises fourteen chapters and sixteen architectural figures. It situates the proposal against planning theory, hierarchical planning, truth maintenance, cognitive architectures, distributed cognition, provenance, capability security, graph engineering, long-term memory, and contemporary agent systems. It concludes with worked examples, falsification tests, and canonical definitions. The individual mechanisms are not claimed as new; the contribution is their architectural synthesis around a persistent semantic center. Version 1.0. Research reviewed through 17 October 2026. articles.title: Switching intention toward conversational AI for health information seeking: a push–pull–mooring analysis
articles.abstract: Introduction With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, users are increasingly turning to conversational AI for health information seeking. This study applies the Push-Pull-Mooring (PPM) framework to explain users' switching intention from social media to conversational AI for comparable health-information-seeking tasks. Methods Survey data were collected from 2,876 Chinese respondents. Structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) were used to examine the associations of push, pull, and mooring factors with switching intention. Results Health information overload and cyberchondria were positively associated with dissatisfaction with social media, which was positively associated with switching intention. Perceived personalization and perceived anonymity were positively associated with flow experience during conversational AI use, which was also positively associated with switching intention. In contrast, medical AI resistance bias and switching costs were negatively associated with switching intention. The fsQCA results further showed that high switching intention was more likely to emerge under configurations characterized by strong pull and weak mooring conditions, whereas low switching intention was typically associated with high mooring conditions. Discussion The findings highlight the joint roles of push, pull, and mooring factors in shaping users' switching intention and demonstrate that switching intention can arise through multiple asymmetric configurations.

articles.title: A Student-Centric Conversational Path-Derivation System for Academic Decision Structuring
articles.abstract: Picking an academic field is a common dilemma among students, particularly since it entails making a choice from different programs, institutions, and career paths.Most of the educational chatbots that already exist just provide basic question answering and hardly ever take into account a student's interests, strengths, or future goals, thus making them less effective.This paper presents a system that essentially places the student at the core of the decision-making process in academic choices through conversation, that is a Student-Centric Conversational Path Derivation System.The system starts a conversation with the students in an engaging way and during the conversation, it collects in stages the necessary information such as their educational background, favourite subjects, skills, limitations, and career aspirations.Instead of giving instant answers, it first interprets the input data and examines the different academic paths in terms of how well the student fits them, the eligibility, the practicability, and the alignment with the career goals.After the analysis, a suitable academic pathway supported by a comprehensive rationale is presented to the student.By leveraging human-like conversation with systematic decision analysis, the method enables students to derive their academic paths with assurance, full knowledge, and a high degree of personalization.

articles.title: From few‐shot learning to data‐efficient intelligence
articles.abstract: Abstract Modern artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable progress by scaling data, model size, and computation. Yet scaling alone does not resolve one of the most fundamental gaps between machine and human intelligence: the ability to learn, adapt, and act from limited experience. This limitation is especially visible when labeled examples, expert feedback, user interactions, or real‐world trials are scarce, costly, or dynamically changing. Humans can often grasp a new concept, adapt to a new goal, or personalize behavior after only a few examples or interactions, but many AI systems remain fragile under the same conditions. My research studies data‐efficient generalization: how learning systems can acquire useful priors, adapt to new tasks, and reuse limited experience under bounded supervision. In this article, I trace a continuous research path from few‐shot learning to meta‐learning, in‐context learning, and data‐efficient agentic learning. I first revisit few‐shot learning as a foundational problem and explain how data‐, model‐, and algorithm‐level priors make learning possible when empirical risk minimization is unreliable. I then describe our work on meta‐learning, where task‐level information and parameter‐efficient adaptation enable fast generalization. Next, I discuss in‐context learning in large language models (LLMs) as an implicit form of learning to learn, and show how its connection to classical meta‐learning provides both theoretical insight and practical guidance. Finally, I turn to large language model (LLM)‐based agents, where data efficiency expands beyond labels to include demonstrations, reasoning traces, tool‐use records, preferences, memory, and feedback. Across AI for science, biomedical knowledge discovery, recommendation, search, and personalization, the common thread is simple: more capable AI should extract more learning signal from less experience.

articles.title: The Economic Value of AI-Driven Customer Experience in Digital Business Models
articles.abstract: AI was increasingly revolutionizing digital business models by delivering superior customer experience and creating identifiable financial value. This study sought to understand the economic consequences of AI-enabled customer experience on digital media platforms in terms of consumer mindset, business functionality, and competitive edge. The purpose was to investigate how AI enhances customer interaction, what it contributes economically in terms of cost-cutting and increased profits, as well as identification of challenges, threats, and future trends. A quantitative research design was adopted, and a structured questionnaire was distributed to 250 users of digital business service. The results demonstrated that AI was found to facilitate increased customer satisfaction, transaction time saving and personalization and thus led to greater inclination of spending and loyalty. A ranking analysis showed that the most valued outcomes were cost savings and customer satisfaction, and the former was found to be the most preferred. Results indicated that the firms that integrated AI had received a more positive brand reputation and competitive advantage than those without. The report found that AI-based customer experience had generated significant economic value, but also encountered challenges in trust, data security and implementation cost continued to be challenging.

articles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing: Consumer Responses, Authenticity, and Governance Challenges
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has moved within a few years from experimental tool to routine instrument in marketing departments, and the academic literature is still catching up with that speed. This chapter offers a structured review of work published between 2020 and 2026 on how GenAI is used in marketing, how consumers respond to it, and which governance questions follow. Drawing on journal articles from marketing, information systems, economics and law, together with regulatory documents from the European Union and Türkiye, the chapter first separates predictive from generative systems and maps their uses in content production, personalization, customer interaction and marketing research. It then organizes the consumer evidence around three recurring themes: task-dependent preference for machine advice, authenticity penalties attached to perceived AI authorship, and the ambiguous effects of humanlike design in service encounters. Field and experimental studies of workplace use point to productivity gains that are uneven across workers, while creativity research shows a tension between individual output quality and collective diversity. The chapter also discusses hallucination, representational bias, privacy and dark patterns, the energy demand of large models, and the transparency duties introduced by the EU Artificial Intelligence Act alongside Turkish data protection guidance. Much of the evidence rests on short online experiments and on firms in North America and Europe, so conclusions about long-term behavior and about Türkiye remain provisional. The chapter closes with a research agenda on longitudinal field designs, disclosure formats, cross-cultural replication and the measurement of environmental cost in marketing operations. For managers, the evidence suggests that the source, tone and disclosure of generated content matter as much as its quality.

articles.title: Who Uses Conversational AI and Why? Distinct User Profiles and Their Links to Personality, Attachment, and Well-Being
articles.abstract: With the increasing use of conversational AI (CAI) agents, such as ChatGPT, public concern about their social implications has grown. Understanding these implications requires new knowledge about the increasingly diverse motives underlying CAI use, ranging from instrumental purposes, such as work, to personal purposes, including social support and entertainment. However, little is known about the motivational profiles underlying CAI use, how these profiles relate to personality traits and attachment dimensions, or whether they differ in well-being. To address this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 783 CAI users (Mage = 43.46, SD = 13.58). Drawing on Uses and Gratifications (U & G) Theory, we measured key motivations underlying CAI use, including information seeking, task efficiency, personalization, social interaction, and playfulness, and subjected them to latent profile analysis to uncover distinct motivational profiles. Big Five personality traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Conscientiousness, Agreeableness) and attachment styles (Anxious and Avoidant) were examined as predictors of the user profiles. We measured emotional, social, and psychological well-being to understand if these aspects differed across the various user profiles. We identified four distinct profiles of CAI users: Occasional Information Seekers, Utilitarians, Social Engagers, and All-Round Engagers. Neuroticism, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Attachment anxiety were significant predictors of profile membership. Finally, profile membership was associated with all well-being indicators, with All-Round Engagers reporting the highest well-being across all three dimensions and Social Engagers reporting the lowest emotional and psychological well-being. These findings advance our understanding of who engages with CAI and how, with potential implications for well-being.

articles.title: From Operational Disruption to Intelligent Service Operations: A Practitioner Journey with Autonomous AI Agents
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 disruption and subsequent talent mobility exposed important vulnerabilities in traditional service operations. Organizations relying heavily on individual expertise faced risks to operational continuity when experienced professionals moved roles or left. Although knowledge transfer, standard operating procedures, and documentation remain essential, they do not always capture the contextual knowledge developed through years of resolving incidents. The resulting gaps can affect service quality, turnaround time, operating costs, and user experience. This chapter examines how human-AI collaboration can strengthen operational resilience and knowledge continuity in service operations. It draws on the practitioner journey behind IgnitronX.AI, a cloud-native multi-agent platform developed to address enterprise operational challenges using generative AI and agentic AI. Its architecture supports service teams by surfacing similar historical incidents, recommending potential resolutions, enabling knowledge discovery, summarizing operational records, and providing sentiment insights. The objective is not to replace human expertise but to augment it. The implementation journey demonstrated that technology alone cannot deliver sustainable value. Data quality emerged as a critical constraint, alongside security, confidentiality, framework and model selection, operating-cost management, governance, and stakeholder adoption. The experience also reinforced that organizations should first understand the business problem, simplify processes, remove waste, and make deliberate build-versus-buy decisions. Through this reflective practitioner case, the chapter offers leaders practical insights into intelligent operations that preserve organizational knowledge, strengthen service continuity, and create the potential for improved productivity, operational efficiency, and user experience through responsible human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: Current applications of artificial intelligence for advancing agriculture, sustainability and climate mitigation
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.

articles.title: Augmented Brand Intelligence in Marketing: How Human-AI Complementarity Shapes Consumer-Brand Interactions
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing and consumer-brand interactions through personalization, efficiency, prediction, and scalability. Its expanding role, however, raises a more fundamental question: what does AI add to consumer interactions, and where does human involvement remain especially valuable? Using signaling theory as its principal explanatory lens, this chapter develops the concept of augmented brand intelligence to explain how human and artificial intelligence can function as complementary sources of brand signals in consumer-facing interactions. A structured critical synthesis of research on AI in marketing, human-AI collaboration, consumer responses to AI, signaling, and consumer-brand relationships suggests that human involvement can signal relational capability through empathy, contextual judgment, relational understanding, and authentic engagement, whereas AI can signal technological capability through efficiency, personalization, analytical capability, and innovation. The framework distinguishes signal complementarity from signal congruence: complementarity concerns whether human and AI signals contribute distinct, nonredundant information about the brand or the capabilities it offers, whereas congruence concerns whether those signals convey compatible meanings about the brand. Complementary signals are expected to reduce perceived information asymmetry more strongly when congruence is high, because consumers can integrate distinct information into a coherent interpretation of the brand. The framework is illustrated across five application domains: customer service, personalization, brand communication, recommendation systems, and customer relationship management. By moving beyond a substitution-focused perspective, the chapter explains how the orchestration of human and AI capabilities can create credible, trusted, and relationally meaningful consumer experiences, and concludes with managerial guidance and an agenda for empirical research across diverse consumer, brand, and technological contexts.

articles.title: Exploring generative AI appropriation in Colombian adults’ informal English learning
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

articles.title: TrajOnco: a multi-agent framework for temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHR for multi-cancer early detection
articles.abstract: Abstract Accurate estimation of cancer risk from longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) could support earlier detection and improved care, but modeling such complex patient trajectories remains challenging. We present TrajOnco, a training-free, multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework designed for scalable multi-cancer early detection. Using a chain-of-agents architecture with long-term memory, TrajOnco performs temporal reasoning over sequential clinical events to generate patient-level summaries, evidence-linked rationales, and predicted risk scores. We evaluated TrajOnco on de-identified Truveta EHR data across 15 cancer types using matched case-control cohorts, predicting risk of cancer diagnosis at 1 year. In zero-shot evaluation, TrajOnco achieved AUROCs of 0.64–0.80, performing comparably to supervised machine learning in a lung cancer benchmark while demonstrating better temporal reasoning than single-agent LLMs. The multi-agent design also enabled effective temporal reasoning with smaller-capacity models such as GPT-4.1-mini. The groundedness of TrajOnco’s output was supported by human evaluation. Furthermore, TrajOnco’s interpretable reasoning outputs can be aggregated to reveal population-level risk patterns that align with established clinical knowledge. These findings highlight the potential of multi-agent LLMs to execute interpretable temporal reasoning over longitudinal EHRs, advancing both scalable multi-cancer early detection and clinical insight generation.

articles.title: OpenCommons: A Distributed, Meaning-Indexed Concept Commons for Accelerating Scientific and Algorithmic Discovery in AI Agents
articles.abstract: When swarms of autonomous AI agents solve complex coding and scientific discovery tasks, they reset their memory between sessions. As a result, agents waste compute repeatedly re-deriving the same mathematical algorithms from scratch while copying subtle numerical errors. Existing skill libraries either store unverified code that spreads bugs across the swarm, or rely on formal verification systems that attempt to translate ordinary Python code into pure mathematical equations—a process that succeeds on only 12.5% of imperative scientific programs. We present OpenCommons, a decentralized concept commons that catalogs algorithms by what they actually compute rather than their surface syntax. By executing functions against a small suite of boundary test inputs, OpenCommons identifies equivalent implementations in less than a millisecond, achieving 100% coverage of native scientific code. An asynchronous peer-review engine stress-tests contributed code in the background, quarantining all defective submissions across six adversarial defect classes with zero false alarms. When evaluated on live language models solving scientific discovery tasks, retrieving verified concept cards increases first-attempt success from 33.3% to 83.3% while preventing the propagation of subtle bugs. Across multi-wave research horizons, this verified shared library reduces cumulative discovery cost by 12.67x, providing a dependable foundation for collective machine intelligence.

articles.title: World–Self–Mutual Models: An Adaptive Framework for Switching Between Self-Learning and Collaborative Learning
articles.abstract: Learning systems face a fundamental architectural choice: whether to improve their internal knowledge and predictive capabilities through independent learning or to acquire additional information and capabilities through collaboration with other learning systems. Permanent reliance on either strategy can be inefficient. Self-learning preserves autonomy and reduces communication overhead but may limit access to complementary knowledge. Collaborative learning can improve information coverage and knowledge acquisition but introduces communication costs, coordination requirements, information inconsistency, and dependence on external learning partners. This paper proposes the World–Self–Mutual Adaptive Learning Framework (WSM-ALF), a conceptual architecture that integrates world models, self models, and mutual models to support adaptive switching between self-learning and collaborative learning. The world model represents environmental states, dynamics, and predicted consequences; the self model estimates the learning system's internal knowledge, capabilities, uncertainty, and limitations; and the mutual model represents relationships between learning systems, including complementary capabilities, information dependencies, communication reliability, and expected collaboration benefits. A meta-learning controller estimates the relative utility of independent and collaborative learning and selects the learning mode according to expected improvement, uncertainty reduction, resource consumption, and collaboration risk. The framework further introduces a transition mechanism that permits repeated switching rather than enforcing a permanently independent or permanently collaborative architecture. A mathematical formulation, an operational algorithm, a model-update protocol, and a comparative experimental design are presented. The proposed framework is intended for non-LLM learning systems, including model-based reinforcement learning, embodied agents, robotics, simulation systems, and autonomous scientific discovery. Its principal contribution is a unified design hypothesis in which the decision to learn independently or collaboratively becomes an explicit, state-dependent control problem within a world-model-based architecture. The framework remains a research proposal whose effectiveness, novelty relative to specific prior systems, and generalizability require empirical evaluation.

articles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of an AI-Assisted Personalized Learning Pathway in Mobile-Supported Online Physical Education
articles.abstract: This study evaluates the effectiveness of an AI-assisted personalized learning pathway in mobile-supported online physical education. To overcome issues of homogeneous content and delayed feedback, a system integrating cognitive knowledge, physical fitness, and motor skills was developed. Reinforcement learning dynamically adapted learning pathways, while edge-based computer vision enabled real-time feedback on low-end mobile devices. A randomized controlled trial with 120 students over eight weeks compared the proposed system to conventional video-based instruction. Results showed low inference latency (34.8 ms) and a 61.2% reduction in movement variability. NASA-TLX scores revealed lower mental demand and frustration, with high learner engagement. The findings highlight the effectiveness of AI-assisted personalization and mobile feedback in improving learning outcomes and experiences in online physical education.

articles.title: Post-Purchase Emotional Collapse: LLM-Assisted Analysis of Online Consumer Complaint Narratives
articles.abstract: Online shopping environments involve interactions shaped by trust, responsiveness, speed, and personalization. When post-purchase service failures occur, customer reactions may extend beyond dissatisfaction to cumulative emotional disruption, including regret, frustration, exhaustion, perceived betrayal, and trust erosion. Despite extensive research on service failure and complaint behavior, limited attention has been given to progressive emotional breakdowns across digital consumption journeys. Addressing this gap, the study introduces post-purchase emotional collapse (PPEC), defined as a cumulative emotional breakdown resulting from repeated service failures and unresolved negative experiences across customer touchpoints. Using a qualitative content analysis design, the study analyzes 1,000 consumer complaints from sikayetvar.com via Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted emotional coding, touchpoint identification, metaphor analysis, and narrative classification, with human validation on a subsample. Findings suggest delivery failures as the most frequently coded rupture point, with anger, disappointment, and regret as the most frequently coded primary emotions. Complaint narratives include metaphors of deception, battle, and destruction, which are compatible with a reading of cumulative deterioration. The study contributes by conceptualizing PPEC and illustrating the potential and the limits of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis in consumer research; it also offers managerial implications for emotionally responsive complaint management systems.

articles.title: A Multi-Agent AI Optimization System for Improving Rig Utilization and Production Gains in the Burgan Field
articles.abstract: Abstract Scheduling a fleet of workover rigs across a mature giant field requires balancing production objectives against a dense web of operational constraints: artificial lift readiness, material availability, location doability, site and pad access, and rig–well compatibility. In the Greater Burgan complex, this forward planning has historically been built and maintained manually in the well delivery management (WDM) system, an in-house rig-scheduling application in which of the order of ten stakeholder teams continuously record and revise workover activities and their constraints. Across a typical year, the programme spans on the order of 500 workover wells and roughly 40 active rigs; distributing that fleet across the candidate wells and their ordered sequences yields a combinatorial space of astronomical size, on the order of hundreds of septillions of feasible arrangements and beyond, that cannot be searched by hand. This paper describes the design, deployment, and field evaluation of a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) scheduling system introduced by the Operator's Integration Excellence team to optimize the 90-day forward plan across the full workover operation of approximately 40 rigs and 200 workover wells. The system decomposes scheduling across cooperating agents: data preprocessing, rig–well resource matching, constraint validation, schedule optimization by a genetic algorithm adapted to the Operator's scheduling rules and operating over short- and long-term memory, execution monitoring, and feedback, with a human-in-the-loop review and approval workflow retained throughout. Planners select one of two objective modes (maximize production gain or meet a specified production target) while the optimizer enforces stability rules that protect active and next-scheduled jobs, group multi-well sites, and honor rig–well compatibility. Performance was evaluated by comparing manually prepared schedules against system-optimized schedules over identical planning inputs and, separately, through historical validation (backtesting) over rolling 90-day look-back windows. To respect data-confidentiality requirements, production results are reported in normalized form and absolute volumes are withheld. In a field-wide evaluation, the optimized schedule increased the projected 90-day production gain by 16% over the manual baseline, an advantage that compounded across the horizon, while fleet-average rig idle time fell by 46% and schedule preparation collapsed from about ten days of manual coordination to minutes of computation. The paper presents the constraint taxonomy and scheduling logic in transferable form and outlines an ongoing extension to new-drill planning, where injector–producer relationships, injection timing, and rig-contract capability introduce additional considerations.

articles.title: Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching for Large Language Models
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-term interaction, task continuity, experience reuse, and collaborative problem-solving. However, existing memory architectures often emphasize individual memory management, shared memory repositories, or predefined collaboration strategies. These approaches leave an important design question: how can multiple memory perspectives generated by the same model coexist with memories maintained by heterogeneous models, while the system adaptively determines when to operate independently and when to exchange information? This paper proposes Parallel-World Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching (PW-ASMS), a unified framework that combines parallel memory worlds, adaptive self-memory, shared-memory collaboration, and cross-model memory integration. Parallel memory worlds are created by assigning different memory orientations to instances of the same underlying model. Each world independently selects, organizes, updates, and retrieves experiences according to its designated orientation. A dynamic controller subsequently determines whether an agent should rely on its own memory, exchange information with other parallel worlds, consult a shared memory repository, or combine these operations. The framework also supports heterogeneous LLMs whose memories can contribute complementary information to a common collaborative process. The proposed architecture consists of parallel memory worlds, individual memory stores, a governed shared memory layer, a memory evaluation module, and an adaptive switching controller. A utility-based decision mechanism considers task relevance, information novelty, confidence, memory consistency, communication cost, privacy constraints, and expected downstream benefit. The framework is designed to reduce unnecessary information exchange while preserving opportunities for collaborative knowledge acquisition. We formulate research questions, operational procedures, evaluation metrics, and experimental comparisons to assess its effectiveness. The paper provides a conceptual and methodological foundation for investigating adaptive memory organization in multi-agent LLM systems; its effectiveness remains to be established empirically.

articles.title: In-Parameter Learning: Why Lifelong AI Systems Need More Than Longer Context
articles.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to interact with changing users, tools, and environments over extended periods of time. However, current systems remain largely static: their parameters are fixed during deployment, while new experiences, domain knowledge, corrections, and behavioral adaptations are handled primarily through external memory management and in-context learning. In this position paper, we focus on lifelong AI: AI systems that can continually learn from their long-term experience throughout an extended deployment lifetime. This position paper argues that existing in-context mechanisms are insufficient for lifelong AI, and advocate In-Parameter Learning (IPL) as a necessary complement to In-Context Learning (ICL), referring to mechanisms that allow a deployed model to continually and safely update its parameters during use. More broadly, we aim to renew the community’s attention to in-parameter learning and to recalibrate the overly optimistic expectations placed on in-context learning alone. Our central claim is that future lifelong AI systems should be built around a hybrid paradigm: in-context learning for immediate, provisional, and reversible information, and in-parameter learning for durable, cumulative, and generalizable growth.
